clue.text: Am able to turn' clergyman out?

indicators.note: to turn the words 'I can' over is to rework their letters into a new order

parts.note: 'am able' is 'I can' with the subject spelt out
a curate is an assistant parish clergyman

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they can manage to turn a vicar out of his parish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to turn' rearranges ICAN into INAC; 'out' is used in the sense of a guess or sum that is wrong, and the question mark flags that sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A calculation that is out is wrong, not correct.

clue.text: Island on edge of Atlantic

indicators.note: the edge of a word here means its opening letter only

explanation.surface: A description of a small isle lying where the ocean begins.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the Hebridean isle off western Scotland faces the open Atlantic.
explanation.definitionFit: Iona is a small island of the Inner Hebrides, exposed to the western ocean.

clue.text: Balls for a medal round

parts.note: MM stands for the Military Medal, a British gallantry award
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: Some spheres are awarded to the winner of a medal round in a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' means musket balls or shot, and 'round' is the ring-shaped letter, not a contest stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Lead balls fired from old guns are ammunition, shortened colloquially.

clue.text: Ethical system infamous, in two centuries after Reformation

indicators.note: a re-formation of the letters means building them into a new shape

parts.note: C is a hundred in Roman numerals, so two of them give CC

explanation.surface: Something called infamous comes up when dating events across the two hundred years after the Protestant Reformation.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital R makes 'Reformation' look like the church movement; it is the signal to rearrange INFAMOUS, IN and CC.
explanation.definitionFit: The teaching of Kong Fuzi is a moral and social code for conduct rather than a religion of gods.

clue.text: Poet's ahead of time with right articles

parts.note: 'a' is the indefinite article
'the' is the definite article

explanation.surface: A poet arrives early, carrying the right papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'articles' gives two pieces, both grammatical articles; 'Poet's' marks the word as literary or archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: An old literary word for early, used by Milton for flowers blooming before their season.

clue.text: Host in midsummer?

explanation.surface: Someone wonders who plays host at a summer solstice party.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle of the word 'summer' is MM, and M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so two of them are literally thousands.
explanation.definitionFit: A host is a great multitude, a vast number; and the central letters of the season name are two Roman thousand signs.

clue.text: Employer and unions endeavour to be extremely selective

indicators.note: being selective only at the extremes means choosing just the first and last letters of each word

explanation.surface: Bosses and trade unions are both trying to be very choosy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be extremely selective' tells you to take only the outside letters of 'unions' (US) and 'endeavour' (ER).
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone who employs a tool or service makes use of it.

clue.text: Beat chaser somehow, in the case of cavalryman

indicators.note: somehow suggests the words get put together in some unstated new order

explanation.surface: A rider in a cavalry regiment is told to beat off a pursuer somehow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges the ten letters of BEAT CHASER; 'in the' joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sabretache was a flat leather satchel hung from a cavalry officer's sword belt.

clue.text: Rely on school to 'produce plant

parts.note: to rest on something is to rely on it
Harrow is a famous English public school in north-west London

explanation.surface: Someone trusts a school to grow a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rely on' in the surface is one phrase, but 'Rely' gives REST and 'on' simply sits before 'school'. Harrow is a famous fee-paying school in London.
explanation.definitionFit: A pink-flowered leguminous weed of fields, whose tough roots once stopped harrows.

clue.text: Put-up job

parts.note: normally a rigged swindle, but read literally it is a post for which a candidate has been put up

explanation.definitionFit: Proposing a person formally for an office is putting them up for it.

clue.text: Bird Al gets for making excuses

indicators.note: Al gets the bird to form the excuses word, so taking Al away from that word leaves the bird

parts.note: to plead alibis is to make excuses
taken as written

explanation.surface: Al is given a bird as a reward for coming up with excuses.
explanation.walkthrough: AL plus the answer spells ALIBIS, which works as a verb meaning offers excuses.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-legged wading bird with a curved bill, sacred in ancient Egypt.

clue.text: Written submissions in exceptional instances

explanation.surface: Lawyers put in written arguments only in unusual matters.
explanation.walkthrough: In English law a special case is a written statement of agreed facts submitted to a court for its ruling on the law.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal term for statements of facts put to the court; and plainly, situations that are out of the ordinary.

clue.text: Political address certainly in standard English

explanation.surface: A political speech is delivered, surely, in proper English.
explanation.walkthrough: The monarch's speech opens each session of the UK Parliament; and the speech of the Queen was taken as the model of correct English.
explanation.definitionFit: The monarch reads out the government programme at the opening of Parliament; and royal speech means standard, correct pronunciation, like 'the Queen's English'.

clue.text: TV is dearer alternative for him 7.30.

indicators.note: an alternative form of the words is another arrangement of their letters

explanation.surface: A man is told that television is the costlier option for him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alternative' rearranges TV IS DEARER. The definition is just 'him': the clue as a whole describes the person who finds TV the dearer way to promote goods.
explanation.definitionFit: The man meant is a promoter who pays to publicise products, for whom television costs more than print.

clue.text: Watch part of match on horse

parts.note: a football match is played in two halves
a hunter is a horse bred for riding to hounds

explanation.surface: A spectator watches part of a game while sitting on a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' looks like a verb; it is the pocket watch. 'on' places the first piece before the second in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A pocket watch whose lid has a small window so the time shows through when closed.

clue.text: Language two boys used about redhead

indicators.note: about means placed around, so one boy's name surrounds the letter

parts.note: David is a boy's name
the head of the word red is its first letter, R
Ian is another boy's name

explanation.surface: Two lads speak a language around a ginger-haired friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'redhead' is one word, but only its head, the first letter, is used; 'two boys' supplies two separate names, and 'about' puts the first around that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A family of tongues of southern India, including Tamil and Telugu.

clue.text: First person in two cases includes summary that's vague

parts.note: the first person singular in the subject case is I

indicators.note: one word includes another by holding it inside itself

parts.note: the first person singular in the object case is me
a precis is a brief summary of a text

explanation.surface: The leading figure in two legal cases sums up in a way that is woolly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First person in two cases' is a grammar joke: the subject and object forms of the first person pronoun. ME 'includes' PRECIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unclear and lacking exactness, loose in detail.

clue.text: It doesn't reduce don's standing, 'however

parts.note: a professorship raises an academic's status, though a seat on which the don sits does stop him standing

explanation.definitionFit: A university professorship is named after a seat, the piece of furniture.

clue.text: Impish model fine in part

indicators.note: in part says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A mischievous fashion model is fine in her role.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the end of 'model' into 'fine'.
explanation.definitionFit: Like a sprite of folklore: mischievous and small.

clue.text: Nut-tree I chop as it is damaged

indicators.note: damage to the phrase breaks its letters up so they can be reassembled

explanation.surface: A woodcutter admits to chopping a nut tree, which is now damaged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is damaged' rearranges I CHOP AS IT.
explanation.definitionFit: A small tree bearing green-kernelled nuts, native to western Asia.

clue.text: Brilliant strokes can make Ted runs, of course

indicators.note: these letters can make something else when shuffled into a new order

parts.note: R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A batsman called Ted scores runs with brilliant shots, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can make' rearranges TED, R and OF COURSE. The cricket surface misleads: 'strokes' are feats, not shots.
explanation.definitionFit: A tour de force is a feat of great skill; here in the plural, masterly achievements.

clue.text: Pound, formerly sovereign

parts.note: once means at some time in the past
R stands for rex or regina, king or queen

explanation.surface: A pound coin was once called a sovereign.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface plays on the sovereign as a gold coin; here it is the monarch. A oncer was British slang for a one-pound note.
explanation.definitionFit: Old British slang for a one-pound note.

clue.text: City renowned for its listed building

definitions.text: City renowned for its listed building

parts.words: City renowned for its listed building
parts.note: listed usually means protected as heritage, but here it means tilted, like a ship that lists

explanation.definitionFit: The Italian city whose bell tower famously leans.

clue.text: Fever, finishing off Romeo's kinsman

indicators.note: only the finish of the name is kept, with its opening chopped away

parts.note: Romeo's family in Shakespeare's play are the Montagues

explanation.surface: A fever kills off one of Romeo's relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo's family name in Romeo and Juliet is Montague; only its last four letters are used.
explanation.definitionFit: A malarial illness marked by shivering bouts and high temperature.

clue.text: Third man's replacement positioned at end of pitch

parts.note: to set something is to position it

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A cricket substitute at third man is placed at the far end of the field.
explanation.walkthrough: Third man is a cricket fielding position, but here the 'third man' is Adam's third son, given in place of the murdered Abel.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, Adam's third son was granted in place of Abel.

clue.text: Considering girl's language less than polite

parts.note: Di is a girl's name, short for Diana, here with the possessive
cussing is swearing, a rude kind of speech

explanation.surface: Someone is thinking about a girl's rather rude way of speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Considering' is the participle 'thinking over', matching the -ING form of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Talking over a matter means thinking about it carefully.

clue.text: Thin, like Jonson

explanation.surface: A comment that a person is slender, like the playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson's tombstone in Westminster Abbey reads 'O rare Ben Jonson'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin air has low density; and the epitaph on the playwright's grave calls him exceptional.

clue.text: Growing peace of mind

explanation.surface: Calm of mind is increasing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Growing' is a noun here: something that grows, a plant, namely the wild pansy.
explanation.definitionFit: The wild pansy is a garden flower; and tranquillity of spirit is ease of the inner self.
